newsitem.title: USA: ADM to settle two lawsuits for $65 million.
newsitem.headline: ADM to settle two lawsuits for $65 million.

text.p: Archer Daniels Midland Co agreed to settle two pending lawsuits -- one concerning a federal antitrust probe into citric acid and the other alleged securities law violations -- for a total of $65 million.
Without admitting any wrongdoing, the company said it would pay $35 million to settle the citric acid lawsuit, which had been filed in U.S. District Court in Northern California.

The citric acid case stemmed from a federal probe of alleged price-fixing in world markets for citric acid, a food additive; high fructose corn syrup, a beverage and food sweetener; and lysine, a livestock feed additive.
Officials of Decatur, Illinois-based ADM, one of the world's largest processors of corn and oilseeds, did not return telephone calls late Friday.
Shares in the company closed unchanged Friday at 19. The company is scheduled to hold its annual meeting October 17.

ADM acknowledged on September 25 that the U.S. Justice Department was considering indictments against the company and two of its executives in connection with the price-fixing investigation. The two executives cited by ADM as possible targets of the probe were vice chairman Michael Andreas and group vice president Terrance Wilson.
Andreas is the son of ADM chairman Dwayne Andreas. Wilson is in charge of the company's corn refining operations.

The shareholders' class-action lawsuit, which ADM said it would settle for $30 million without admitting wrongdoing, was filed in central Illinois by shareholders who alleged they had paid artificially inflated prices for the company's stock.
Both settlements are positive developments for ADM, but likely will force ADM to take a charge against earnings, said Everen Securities industry analyst Richard Elam.
"These do seem to be further progress in resolving the company's legal problems," Elam said.
The company said in a recent proxy statement that it had set aside legal reserves to cover the possible settlement of a case related to the lysine portion of the price-fixing probe.

But it said, "Because of the early stage of the other investigations and putative class actions, the ultimate outcome of these matters cannot presently be determined. Accordingly, no provision for any liability that may result therefrom has been made."
If no reserve has been made to cover the settlements announced Friday, Elam said, then ADM will likely take a $0.12 per share charge against earnings in the second quarter.
The company reported earnings in the second quarter of fiscal 1996, ended December 31, 1995, of $0.43 per share and for all of fiscal 1996, ended June 30, 1996, of $1.33 per share.

The settlements announced Friday by ADM concern two civil cases that stemmed from the federal price-fixing probe. They follow an agreement made earlier this year to pay $25 million to settle an antitrust suit brought by lysine customers.
These and other lawsuits were filed after ADM disclosed in late June 1995 that it had been subpoenaed by federal authorities for testimony and documents as part of the probe.

A source close to the investigation said ADM's settlements indicate a willingness by the agribusiness giant to put allegations of antitrust behind it. "They really want to start to get this behind them," the source said.
No charges have been filed in the federal probe, but sources close to the investigation say talks are continuing between ADM and the Justice Department regarding a possible plea agreement.
